claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation during sustained loading is driven by dynamic evolution of dislocation structures.
Evolving dislocation structures locally induce short-range chemical ordering at nanoscale layer interfaces.
Interfacial short-range chemical ordering reduces barriers to subsequent dislocation motion.
The reduction in dislocation-motion barriers accelerates creep.
The starting material is a nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer with a chemically disordered, high-strength microstructure.
The starting multilayer has well-defined coherent interfaces.
A pretreatment can suppress, disrupt, or randomize inherent short-range order while otherwise yielding a similar multilayer.
The selected high-temperature, moderate-to-high-stress creep conditions preserve the multilayer architecture.
Temperature and applied stress influence creep behavior and the contribution of dislocation motion in high-entropy alloys.
Dislocations preferentially accumulate and interact at multilayer interfaces during creep.
Interfacial dislocation interactions trigger atomic rearrangements that form short-range-order domains.
Short-range-order domains create locally softened regions in which dislocation glide is easier.
The interfacial short-range-order parameter will increase during sustained loading.
High-resolution TEM or diffraction can detect and quantify the proposed interfacial short-range-order evolution.
Local yield strength will decrease as interfacial short-range order evolves.
Creep rate will accelerate relative to the homogeneous, minimally ordered baseline.
The proposed mechanism is specific to creep in nanoscale multilayers and may not apply to bulk high-entropy alloys.
Recovery-dominated loading regimes may suppress or replace the proposed mechanism.
A lack of significant differences between pretreated and as-deposited samples in ordering, dislocation behavior, and creep response would falsify the hypothesis.
